title: Asking Price
passage:
A seaside season does not end on a date. It thins, and then one week the chairs stay in. In a good July week three hundred and forty of them go out on the east beach at a pound and ten pence a day, and the pitch does a ___(1)___ trade from eleven until the light goes. On the last Tuesday of September the racks under the arches held three hundred and thirty-six chairs that had ___(2)___ there since breakfast, and the tin took four pounds forty.

What the pitch charges for and what it does are not the same thing. In one hour of that Tuesday its attendant was asked where the lavatory was, whether the tide was coming in, when the last bus left for the station, and whether anybody had handed in a red shoe. She was also asked to watch a bag, a thing you ask of somebody who will still be there.

The hire is the whole of the transaction, and it has risen by ten pence in a decade. ___(3)___, the pitch is the one staffed thing on the mile between the pier and the sailing club, and Carol Gregson the one person on it who is stationary and paid. She has worked it for nine seasons. The chairs are in two stripe patterns, after a 2019 replacement batch came in the wrong blue, and that is how the stacks are told apart. Pressed on whether she minds the questions, she ___(4)___ that in August they are an obstruction and by late September most of the job.

The town has tried providing the same thing directly. A seafront information point opened on the promenade in 2018, with a counter, a leaflet rack and a paid assistant. It was well signed and it was free, but it was ___(5)___ used, and it shut after its second summer. The leaflets were not the problem. A counter has to be approached, and approaching one is a decision you have to justify; a chair you have paid for has done the approaching for you. Gregson would not put it that way. Asked why people ask her things, she said it is because she stands still and they do not. The racks come in during the second week of October, and the firm that stacks them does the beach huts.
– Desmond Gaddermoor

questions.rationale: Key D. The frame is the fixed English collocation to do a brisk trade, which is what a busy stall or hire pitch does over a stretch of hours; the surrounding clause, from eleven until the light goes, supplies exactly the sustained-busy reading that collocation carries, and brisk is the only one of the four words that combines with trade in that sense. A (hasty) is a collocation misfit: right part of speech, same semantic field, but a hasty trade would describe one transaction done in a hurry, and there is no single transaction in the frame. B (rapid) is the same misfit in a neutral register; rapid trade belongs to markets moving quickly, not to a pitch taking money steadily all afternoon, and it fights the leisurely time adverbial. C (swift) is the near-synonym trap and the one most likely to be chosen by a solver who has resolved the gap to fast and stopped there; English does not put swift with trade in this frame. All four options are single adjectives from the speed-and-briskness field, so nothing but the collocation separates them.

Key B. The frame is chairs that had ___ there since breakfast: a past perfect, a plural subject, no object, and a locative adverb, so it requires the past participle of intransitive LIE, which is lain. A (lie) is the bare form and cannot follow had; it catches a solver who has chosen a meaning rather than a form. C (laid) is the participle of transitive LAY and would need something that had been laid; it is the commonest error in this pair and should collect most of the wrong answers. D (lay) is the simple past of LIE, correct in the chairs lay there but not after the auxiliary had. All four options are forms of the LIE/LAY pair, so meaning alone settles nothing: only the morphology of the perfect selects a single answer.

Key C. The preceding sentence gives what the pitch is transactionally, a chair hire and the price of one, and the gapped sentence gives what it actually amounts to on that mile of beach, so the connective has to mark the move from nominal description to observed reality: In practice. A (In principle) is the polarity mirror of that relation, presenting the staffed-presence fact as the theoretical side of the contrast when the passage offers it as the real one. B (In return) imports a reciprocal exchange the sentence does not contain; nothing is being given back for anything. D (In advance) has no temporal relation available to attach to. All four options are two-word In + noun adverbials that take a comma and a full clause, so shape gives nothing away and the gap turns entirely on which discourse relation the two sentences stand in.

Key A. Pressed on whether she minds sets up a question she is being made to answer, and what follows is a two-sided admission that spoils a flattering reading of her job, so the reporting verb must be one of yielding a point: concedes. B (boasts) is the attitude mirror and would turn an unglamorous admission into a claim of pride. C (volunteers) is contradicted by the frame itself, since nothing can be volunteered that has just been pressed for. D (confesses) is the register trap and the hardest of the three: grammatically perfect and roughly the right direction, but it treats an ordinary working opinion as a guilty secret, a heavier register than either the sentence or the piece supports. All four options are third-person singular present-tense reporting verbs agreeing with the subject she, and all four take a that-clause, so grammar decides nothing and the gap is settled by stance and register.

Key D. The clause is built on an explicit contrast, well signed and free, then but, and the sentence closes with the point shutting after one further summer, so the gap takes the negative pole: barely. A (widely), B (routinely) and C (heavily) are positive-pole adverbs of extent or frequency, and each is what a solver picks who reads the counter, the leaflet rack and the paid assistant as evidence of success and skims the but. B is the mildest of the three and therefore the most tempting, since routinely used would sit comfortably with a staffed municipal counter and does not overclaim. All four options are single -ly adverbs modifying used, so the polarity of the frame is the only thing separating them.
